idiom_name: Proxy handler + WeakMap identity map + Proxy.revocable
implementation_notes: JavaScript has the interception primitive built in: a Proxy takes a handler whose traps cover the fundamental operations (get, set, apply, construct, ...), so a membrane is a handler that wraps arguments on the way in, forwards to the target, and wraps results, callbacks and iterators on the way out; Proxy.revocable() supplies the kill switch, after which every trap throws and the whole membrane is dead at once. What replaces the classic forwarding class is this handler plus a WeakMap identity map (a second map in the other direction when the wrapped side must be recognised) so a given object always yields the same wrapper and nothing is retained. It stays idiomatic rather than native because the engine only supplies the hook - the both-direction wrapping rules, identity map and policy are still hand-written, and there is no maintained membrane package in the ecosystem (Endo ships SES/harden/marshal, not a membrane). When the guest code is hostile, hardening matters: without SES-style lockdown the guest shares the realm's mutable intrinsics and can reach objects the membrane never wrapped.
pitfalls: Traps must respect the target's invariants: a get trap that hides or changes a non-configurable, non-writable property throws a TypeError instead of mediating, and the invariants are checked against the raw target (MDN).

Wrapping is only as good as its completeness - prototype methods, getters that return objects, iterators, error objects and callbacks passed in must all be wrapped, and a single unwrapped route hands the guest the raw graph.

Proxies do not forward private fields: a proxied instance has a different identity and no access to the original object's #private elements, so private-field classes cannot be wrapped transparently (MDN).

Identity is per membrane: skipping the WeakMap lookup breaks === and leaks wrappers, and in a non-locked-down realm a hostile guest can tamper with intrinsics or reach objects through paths the handler never sees (SES exists for this).
